title: Skeena Salmon In-Season Update
text:
Pre-season forecasts

The pre-season forecast for the Total Return of Skeena sockeye in 2026 ranges from 728,000 to 3.3 million (90% confidence range) with a point estimate (p50) of 1.5 million.
On average, Alaskan fisheries take approximately 5-10% of the aggregate sockeye run, but this depends on their pink salmon fisheries and effort, and can be much higher in some years.

Tyee Test Fishery

Information from fisheries and the Tyee test fishery suggest that sockeye are mostly large this year, suggesting a high proportion of 5-year olds.
To date 1,438,984 sockeye are estimated to have passed the Tyee test fishery.
We are past the historical mid-point (peak) of the run through Tyee. While early estimates of final run size were encouraging, the late run-timing forecast is still declining, and the average run-timing forecast has stabilized near 2.3M (1.9M if the run is one week early, and 3.1M if the run is one week late).
The shape of the run-timing curve suggests that the run could be between 1.5M and 2M, and that there was a strong and early start to the run, and that the mid-point of the run was not as strong.
The daily expected run through Tyee at a final run size of 2M and average run timing would be about between 40,000 and 50,0000 over the next few days.
While run-timing is one source of uncertainty in this estimate, catchability is also a large source of uncertainty. Uncertainty due to run-timing will decrease through the season, where the final catchability of the test fishery is only known post-season. The mid-point of the sockeye run is approximately July 24-26.
The Chinook cumulative index is well below the historical median, and just above the recent 5-year mean and 10-year mean, suggesting continued low abundance for Skeena Chinook.
The chum index suggests high abundance relative to historical index values.
Pink salmon are coming through Tyee around the historical median for even-year pink.
The coho index suggests average abundance.
The steelhead index suggests high abundance relative to historical years, with the index tracking the 90th percentile currently.

Babine

The Babine fence started operations on July 15.
Adult and jack sockeye have started coming through the fence in increasing numbers with a total of ~ 96,000 large sockeye through to date, and ~ 3,100 jack to date.

Kitwanga Fence

The Kitwanga fence started operations July 17. Information from the Kitwanga fence will be shared weekly by Gitanyow Fisheries Authority and can be found on the GFA website.

First Nations Food Fisheries

First Nations food fisheries are ongoing in the marine approaches and in-river.

Commercial Fisheries

First Nations demonstration fisheries opened in the marine areas on July 8 and 9 targeting sockeye and are ongoing.
First Nations demonstration fisheries opened in-river July 16 and are ongoing.
Area C gillnet fisheries started July 10 targeting Skeena sockeye. There were openings on July 10/11, 13/14, 16/17, 19/20/21, 23/24/25, 28/29 and August 1/2.
Area A seine fisheries targeting Skeena sockeye opened July 15-19, 22-26, and continue July 29-August 2.

Recreational Fisheries

Recreational fisheries for sockeye in Areas 3-6 opened July 10 with a daily limit of 4 per day.
Recreational fisheries for Skeena sockeye in portions of Region 6 opened July 10 (portions of the Skeena mainstem) and August 1 (Babine Lake, Fulton River, Pinkut Creek) with a daily limit of 2 per day, and increased to a daily limit of 4 per day July 29-Sept 15.
Babine River opened to recreational fishing for sockeye on August 1-31 with a daily limit of 2 per day.
Recreational fisheries for Chinook in Area 3-5 are currently closed, and will open at 1 per day on July 18, and 2 per day on August 1.

Appendix A shows the daily and cumulative run-timing of Tyee since 2000 versus 2024.
Appendix B includes information on run-timing of specific Skeena Conservation Units/stocks.
Appendix C shows all Skeena fisheries notices from 2026.

Sockeye index

Figure 1: Daily (top) and cumulative (bottom) index values for sockeye salmon from 1956-2025 (grey lines). 2026 values are shown in purple, and various percentiles are shown by the grey dashed lines.







Escapement estimates at Tyee
Escapement estimates for sockeye are generated using the Tyee index and a catchability coefficient based on the average of the last 3 years catchability.
The 2025 sockeye escapement estimate at Tyee is shown below and compared to historical escapement data (not including catch as we do not have the historical daily escapement estimate plus catch) (Figure 2)

In-season abundance estimate
Sockeye in-season abundance (TRTC) is estimated through the Tyee test fishery using the cumulative run-to Tyee (escapement past Tyee plus adjusted marine catch estimates) and run-timing. The following table (Table 1) and figure (Figure 5) show estimates of the final forecasted TRTC for average, one-week late, and one-week early run-timing. This does not incorporate variability in the catchability of the Tyee test fishery (which is confirmed post-season).

First Nations Demonstration and Economic Opportunity
First Nations CSAF demonstration fisheries opened on July 8 in 2026. The catch associated with each demonstration fishery is determined using a proportion of the weekly TAC. In 2026, the CTAC approach is being implemented, which means that the catch allocation of the demonstration fishery is no longer directly linked to what the commercial marine fishery catches each week. title: Skeena Salmon In-Season Update
text:
Recreational Fisheries
The following table shows the updated management guidelines for recreational fisheries targeting sockeye in the Skeena watershed as per the 2026-27 North Coast Salmon IFMP. For the 2026 season, the recreational fishery for Skeena Sockeye will open when the estimated Total Return to Canada threshold of 1.05 million Sockeye has been achieved and commercial fisheries are triggered.



Guidelines for Management Actions for Recreational Sockeye Fisheries in the Skeena Watershed



North Coast Recreational Angling Creel Surveys
The North Coast Skeena First Nations Stewardship Society (NCSFNSS) has operated a creel survey program since 2015 in Areas 3 and 4, consisting of access point angler interviews and aerial overflights for the months of June through August (May through August beginning in 2019). Lodge-based recreational effort and harvest are monitored using DFO’s voluntary logbook program.
The following plots show the estimated recreational effort and catch for Chinook and coho salmon and Pacific halibut by year and month, and estimated CPUE for each species by year.
